concepts.title: Modules and Imports
concepts.description: A module is just a .py file that Python executes once and caches, and import/from-import, sys.path, and the __name__ == "__main__" guard together determine what a program actually loads and runs.
learningObjectives: Explain what a module is and what actually happens when it's imported for the first time.
Explain why importing the same module a second time does not re-run its top-level code.
Choose between import module_name and from module_name import name based on the tradeoffs of each.
Explain the role of sys.path in module resolution.
Use the if __name__ == "__main__": guard correctly and explain the bug it prevents.
Recognize the cause of a circular import and describe at least one way to fix it.

sections.heading: A Module Is Just a .py File
sections.body:
A module is just a `.py` file. When you write `import math`, Python locates a file (or, for built-ins like `math`, a compiled extension) that defines `math`'s contents, **executes that file from top to bottom, once**, and makes the resulting namespace (every name defined at the file's top level: functions, classes, variables) available to you as attributes of the module object.

'Executes... once' matters more than it sounds: the first time any code anywhere in your program imports a given module, Python runs that module's top-level code (any print statements, module-level computations, class/function definitions) and then caches the finished module object in a dict called `sys.modules`, keyed by module name. Every subsequent `import that_module` anywhere in the program, even from a different file, does **not** re-run the module's code; it just looks up the already-built module object in `sys.modules` and hands back a reference to that same object.

```python
# counters.py
print("counters.py is running")
count = 0
```

```python
# main.py
import counters
import counters   # does NOT print "counters.py is running" again -- already cached
print(counters.count)
```

This is why module-level code with side effects (opening a file, connecting to a database, printing something) only happens once per program run, no matter how many different files import that module.

sections.heading: import vs. from module_name import name
sections.body:
`import module_name` brings in the module object itself, under the name `module_name` (or an alias, with `import module_name as alias`); you then access anything inside it through attribute access: `math.sqrt(16)`, `counters.count`. This is unambiguous about where a name came from: reading `math.sqrt` at any call site, you know it isn't some locally defined `sqrt`.

`from module_name import specific_name` instead pulls specific names out of the module's namespace and binds them into your current namespace: `from math import sqrt` lets you write `sqrt(16)` directly, with no `math.` prefix. This is more convenient for names you use constantly, but it has a cost: it's easy to accidentally shadow a built-in or an existing name (`from math import log` can collide with a variable named `log` elsewhere in the same file), and it makes it harder to tell, just by reading a bare name, which module it originally came from. `from module_name import *`, which imports everything a module defines, takes this tradeoff to its extreme and is broadly discouraged for that reason: it dumps an unknown set of names into your namespace, any of which might collide with something you already have.

sections.heading: How Python Finds a Module: sys.path
sections.body:
When Python sees `import some_module`, it needs to locate the corresponding file. It does this by searching, **in order**, through a list of directory paths stored in `sys.path`, a plain list of strings you can inspect (`import sys; print(sys.path)`) and even modify at runtime. That list typically includes: the directory containing the script you're running (or the current directory, for the interactive interpreter), a set of standard-library locations bundled with your Python installation, and any site-packages directories where third-party packages installed via pip live (covered in the next concept).

Python checks these directories **in the order they appear** and imports the first matching module it finds. That's the mechanism behind a recurring beginner mistake: naming your own script `random.py` or `json.py` in the same directory as code that does `import random` or `import json`. Because your script's directory is searched first, your file shadows the standard-library module, and all of its real functions disappear, replaced by whatever happens to be in your file. The resulting errors, such as `AttributeError: module 'random' has no attribute 'randint'`, often have nothing obviously to do with a naming collision. (A few modules compiled into the interpreter, like `sys`, are found before `sys.path` is consulted and can't be shadowed this way; whether `math` is one of them depends on how your Python was built.)

sections.heading: if __name__ == "__main__": and Why It Exists
sections.body:
Every module has a built-in variable `__name__` that Python sets automatically, to different values depending on *how* the file started running. If the file is being run directly (`python my_script.py`), Python sets `__name__` to the string `"__main__"` for that run. If the file is instead being *imported* by some other module (`import my_script`), Python sets `__name__` to the module's own name (`"my_script"`) instead.

```python
# my_script.py
def main():
    print("Running as the main program")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

This lets a single file serve two purposes at once: it can be a reusable module that other files import for its functions/classes (in which case `__name__` will be `"my_script"`, the `if` is false, and nothing extra runs), *and* it can be run directly as a standalone script for testing or as an entry point (in which case `__name__` is `"__main__"`, the `if` fires, and `main()` executes). Without this guard, any 'run this as a script' code (a `main()` call, test invocations, a demo print) would also fire every time some other file imports this one for its useful definitions, which is almost never what you want.

sections.heading: The Circular Import Pitfall
sections.body:
A circular import happens when module A imports module B, and module B -- directly or indirectly -- imports module A back, forming a cycle. Because Python registers a module in `sys.modules` before it finishes executing its code, a circular import can catch a module 'half-built': if A is in the middle of running (say, it has only defined its first function so far) when its import of B triggers B to import A back, Python finds A already in `sys.modules` and hands back that half-finished module object, rather than re-running A (which would loop forever) or waiting for it to finish (which the import system doesn't do). B then tries to use something from A that hasn't been defined yet, and you get an `ImportError` or `AttributeError` that can be confusing to track down, since each module looks correct in isolation.

The practical fixes, roughly in order of how much they change your design: move the import so it happens inside a function body instead of at the top of the file, deferring it until the function is called, by which point both modules have usually finished their top-level execution; restructure so the shared functionality both modules need lives in a third module that both of them import, instead of importing each other directly; or treat a circular import as a hint, often the real signal, that the two modules are too tightly coupled and should be redesigned, rather than a purely technical problem to route around.

examples.title: A Module Only Runs Once, No Matter How Many Times It's Imported
examples.code:
# counters.py
print("counters.py is running")
count = 0

def increment():
    global count
    count += 1
    return count

# main.py
import counters
import counters              # does NOT print "counters.py is running" again

print(counters.increment())  # 1
print(counters.increment())  # 2

import other_module          # other_module.py also does `import counters`
# still does not re-print "counters.py is running" -- and other_module sees
# counters.count already at 2, not reset back to 0
examples.explanation: The first import counters anywhere in the program runs counters.py from top to bottom once, printing its message and creating count = 0, then caches the resulting module object in sys.modules under the key 'counters'. Every later import counters, whether it's the second line in main.py or a separate import inside other_module.py, finds 'counters' already in sys.modules and just hands back a reference to the same already-built module object, without running the file again. Because every part of the program that imports counters gets a reference to the SAME object, calling counters.increment() from main.py changes the count that other_module.py would also see if it read counters.count afterward -- there's only ever one counters module in memory for the whole program, not a fresh copy per import.

examples.title: if __name__ == "__main__": in Action
examples.code:
# calculator.py
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print(f"calculator module loaded, __name__ is {__name__!r}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Running calculator.py directly as a script")
    print(add(2, 3))

# Running `python calculator.py` directly prints:
# calculator module loaded, __name__ is '__main__'
# Running calculator.py directly as a script
# 5

# Meanwhile, `import calculator` from another file prints only:
# calculator module loaded, __name__ is 'calculator'
# (the if block never fires -- __name__ is 'calculator', not '__main__')
examples.explanation: The print statement right after the function definitions is NOT inside the if guard, so it always runs on import, in both scenarios; only the value of __name__ printed differs. When calculator.py is run directly, Python sets __name__ to the string '__main__' for that run, so the if condition is true and the script-only code (the second print and the add(2, 3) call) executes. When some other file does import calculator instead, Python sets __name__ to 'calculator', the module's own name, so the condition is false, and only the useful, reusable parts of the file (the add function's definition and the unconditional print) take effect, without also running whatever demo or test code was meant only for running calculator.py as a standalone script.

misconceptions.description: import some_module re-runs that module's top-level code every single time it's imported, in every file that imports it.
misconceptions.clarification: Python caches every module it imports in a dict called sys.modules, keyed by module name, the first time it's imported anywhere in the running program. Every later import of that same module, from the same file or a different one, just retrieves the already-built module object from that cache; it does not re-execute the module's code. This is why a module with a print statement or a database connection at its top level only triggers that side effect once per program run, regardless of how many different files import it.
misconceptions.fact: Python caches every module it imports in a dict called sys.modules, keyed by module name, the first time it's imported anywhere in the running program.

misconceptions.description: from module_name import * is just a convenient shortcut for import module_name -- it saves typing the module prefix, with no other real differences.
misconceptions.clarification: from module_name import * pulls every public name the module defines directly into your current namespace, with no prefix at all, which creates a risk of overwriting an existing name of yours (or one from another import) that shares the same identifier, and there's often no way to tell, just by reading a bare name later in the file, which module it came from. import module_name, by contrast, only adds one name (the module itself) to your namespace, and every name you access through it is unambiguously prefixed (module_name.something), which is why it doesn't carry the same collision risk. Most style guidance treats from module import * as something to avoid in ordinary application code, reserving it for narrow, deliberate cases like re-exporting a curated set of names from a package's own __init__.py.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? Assume config.py and main.py are separate files in the same directory.
exercises.code:
# config.py
print("loading config...")
DEBUG = True

# main.py
import config
import config
print(config.DEBUG)
DEBUG = False
print(config.DEBUG)
hints: How many times does the message "loading config..." actually print, given that config is imported twice in main.py?
DEBUG = False in main.py creates a variable local to main.py's own namespace -- does it touch config.DEBUG at all?
config.DEBUG and the plain name DEBUG (after the reassignment) refer to two separate variables, living in two separate modules' namespaces.
exercises.expectedAnswer: loading config... (only once), then True, then True again. The second import config does not re-run config.py, so "loading config..." prints only once. DEBUG = False creates a new variable named DEBUG in main.py's own namespace -- it does not modify config.DEBUG at all, so config.DEBUG still reads True both times it's printed.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The first import config runs config.py top to bottom, printing 'loading config...' and setting config.DEBUG = True; that module object is then cached in sys.modules. The second import config finds 'config' already cached and does not re-run the file, so the message is not printed again. print(config.DEBUG) then correctly prints True. The line DEBUG = False does NOT reach into config's namespace; it creates a new variable named DEBUG in main.py's own top-level scope, unrelated to config.DEBUG. So the second print(config.DEBUG) still reads config's own DEBUG attribute, which was never touched, and still prints True.

exercises.prompt: utils.py is meant to be imported by other files purely for its calculate_total function, but importing it triggers an unwanted print of "60" as a side effect. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
# utils.py
def calculate_total(prices):
    return sum(prices)

print(calculate_total([10, 20, 30]))   # meant only as a quick manual test while developing

# main.py
from utils import calculate_total
print(calculate_total([1, 2, 3]))
# expected output: just "6"
# actual output: "60" printed first, then "6"
hints: The print(calculate_total([10, 20, 30])) line inside utils.py runs whenever the file is executed -- does that include when it's merely imported by another file?
Is there anything in utils.py that distinguishes 'this file is being run directly, as a script' from 'this file is being imported for its functions'?
There's a specific if-guard, based on a built-in variable, meant exactly for code that should only run when a file is executed directly.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original utils.py has an unconditional print(calculate_total([10, 20, 30])) at its top level, with nothing to distinguish 'run directly' from 'imported elsewhere', so that line executes every time the module is loaded, including when main.py does from utils import calculate_total purely to reuse the function. Wrapping it in if __name__ == "__main__": means that line only runs when utils.py is executed directly (where __name__ would be "__main__"), not when it's imported by another module (where __name__ is "utils" instead, making the condition false). After the fix, importing calculate_total from main.py no longer triggers the leftover manual test print, and print(calculate_total([1, 2, 3])) outputs just 6.

assessments.prompt: Two different files in the same running program both write `import config` at some point. How many times does config.py's top-level code actually execute?
options: Once per file that imports it -- so twice, in this case
Once per line that says import config anywhere in the program
Zero times, unless something inside config.py is explicitly called afterward
Once total, the first time any file in the program imports it
assessments.explanation: Python caches every module in sys.modules the first time it's imported anywhere in the running program, keyed by module name. Every subsequent import of that same module, from the same file or a different one, just retrieves the cached module object rather than re-running the file. So config.py's top-level code executes once in total, regardless of how many files, or how many import statements across the whole program, reference it. The “Once per file that imports…” and “Once per line that says import config…” options both describe re-running the module once per import statement, which is what the sys.modules cache prevents; the “Zero times, unless something inside config.py…” option is wrong because importing a module DOES execute its top-level code immediately, whether or not anything inside it is explicitly called afterward.

assessments.prompt: A module named shared_state.py defines a module-level variable: `active_users = []`. Two other files, file_a.py and file_b.py, both write `import shared_state` near the top, at different points in the program's execution. file_a.py runs first and does `shared_state.active_users.append("amy")`. Later, file_b.py runs and reads `shared_state.active_users`. What does file_b.py see, and why, based on how Python's import system works?
assessments.modelAnswer: file_b.py sees ['amy']: the mutation made by file_a.py is visible. Even though shared_state is imported separately in two files, Python's import caching (via sys.modules) means both import statements, wherever and whenever they run, refer to the same module object in memory. There is only one shared_state module in the running program, built the first time it's imported and reused by every later import. Since active_users is a mutable list living as an attribute of that one module object, and file_a.py's append() mutates the list in place (rather than reassigning shared_state.active_users to a new list), any code that later accesses shared_state.active_users, including file_b.py, sees the mutated list with amy's entry. That's why modules can be used (deliberately, and carefully) as a lightweight way to share mutable state across a program, and also why unintended shared module state can cause confusing bugs.

assessments.prompt:
```python
from math import log

log = 10
print(log(2.718))
```
What happens?
options: 10, because log is now just a variable holding that value
Approximately 1.0, since log computes the natural logarithm of 2.718
TypeError: 'int' object is not callable
NameError: name 'log' is not defined
assessments.explanation: `from math import log` binds the name `log` in the current namespace to the `math` module's log function. But `log = 10` immediately rebinds that same name to the integer `10`. Nothing protects a `from`-imported name from being overwritten by an ordinary assignment, since both live in the same namespace. By the time `log(2.718)` runs, `log` no longer refers to the function at all; it's `10`, and trying to call an int like a function raises `TypeError: 'int' object is not callable`. This is the collision risk `from module import name` carries that a plain `import module` (accessed as `module.log`) would not.

assessments.prompt: A developer creates a file named `random.py` in the same directory as their main script, intending it to hold their own unrelated helper functions. Their main script does `import random` and then calls `random.randint(1, 10)`, expecting the standard library's function. What actually happens?
options: It likely fails (e.g. AttributeError), because import random finds the developer's own random.py first -- the current directory is searched before the standard library -- so the real randint almost certainly isn't defined there
Python merges the developer's random.py and the standard library's random module into one combined namespace automatically
Python always prefers the standard library module over any same-named file in the current directory, so it works exactly as intended
Python raises ImportError immediately, refusing to import any module that shares a name with a standard library module
assessments.explanation: sys.path is searched in order, and the directory containing the running script is typically searched before the standard-library locations. Because the developer's own random.py sits in that earlier-searched directory, `import random` resolves to their file, not the real standard-library module, shadowing it. Unless their own random.py happens to define a function named randint with matching behavior (unlikely, since it wasn't intended as a random-number module at all), calling random.randint(1, 10) fails, typically with an AttributeError, in a way that looks unrelated to the actual cause: an accidental naming collision with a standard-library module.

assessments.prompt:
A file named `report.py` contains only this at its top level:
```python
print(__name__)
```
What gets printed if you run `python report.py` directly from the terminal, versus if another file does `import report`?
options: 'report' in both cases
'__main__' when run directly
'__main__' in both cases
'report' when run directly; '__main__' when imported
assessments.explanation: Python sets a module's `__name__` differently depending on how that file started running. When a file is executed directly (`python report.py`), Python sets `__name__` to the special string `"__main__"` for that run. When the same file is instead loaded via `import report` from somewhere else, Python sets `__name__` to the module's own name, `"report"`, instead. This is the mechanism the `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard relies on to distinguish 'I'm being run as a script' from 'I'm being imported for my definitions.'

concepts.title: Packages and pip
concepts.description: A package is a directory of related modules that Python can import as one unit, pip is the standard tool for installing third-party packages from PyPI, and requirements.txt records what a project depends on so it can be reproduced elsewhere.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between a module and a package.
Install, upgrade, and uninstall a third-party package using pip.
Explain the purpose of requirements.txt and generate one for a project.
Describe, in broad terms, what PyPI is and why installing an unfamiliar package carries some inherent trust risk.

sections.heading: Package vs. Module: Directories vs. Files
sections.body:
A **module** is a single `.py` file, as covered in the previous concept. A **package** is one level up: a *directory* of Python code that Python treats as a single importable unit, typically containing multiple modules (and possibly sub-packages) organized together. What conventionally marks a directory as a package is an `__init__.py` file inside it. Historically this file was *required*; modern Python (3.3+) also supports 'namespace packages' without `__init__.py` in some situations, but an (even empty) `__init__.py` remains the clear, conventional signal that 'this directory is a package,' and it's the place to put code that should run once when the package is imported, or to control what a plain `import my_package` exposes.

```
my_project/
    shapes/
        __init__.py
        circle.py
        square.py
    main.py
```

Here, `shapes` is a package containing two modules, `circle` and `square`. From `main.py`, you could write `from shapes import circle` and then `circle.area(5)`, or `from shapes.circle import area` to pull the function directly. Packages let projects and libraries organize dozens or hundreds of modules into a coherent, navigable structure instead of dumping every `.py` file flat into one directory.

sections.heading: Installing Third-Party Code with pip
sections.body:
Most third-party functionality (HTTP clients, data analysis libraries, web frameworks, testing tools) doesn't ship with Python itself; it's distributed as packages you install separately, using **pip**, Python's standard package installer. `pip install requests` downloads the `requests` package (and anything it itself depends on) from the Python Package Index and installs it somewhere on your `sys.path` -- typically a `site-packages` directory -- so that any `import requests` in your code can find it, following the same module-resolution mechanism from the previous concept.

Other common pip operations worth knowing early: `pip install package_name==2.1.0` installs a specific version rather than whatever's newest; `pip install --upgrade package_name` installs the latest version over an existing one; `pip uninstall package_name` removes it; `pip list` shows what's currently installed in whichever Python environment pip is currently pointed at (a detail that becomes important in the next concept); `pip show package_name` gives details about an installed package, including its own dependencies.

sections.heading: requirements.txt and Reproducibility
sections.body:
A `requirements.txt` file is a plain text list of package names -- usually with version constraints -- that a project depends on, one per line: `requests==2.31.0`, `pandas>=2.0`, and so on. Its purpose is **reproducibility**: instead of verbally telling every other developer, or your future self on a new machine, 'oh, you'll also need to install these five packages, in roughly these versions,' you commit `requirements.txt` alongside your code, and anyone can recreate an equivalent set of dependencies with a single command: `pip install -r requirements.txt`.

You can generate a first-pass version of this file automatically from whatever's currently installed with `pip freeze > requirements.txt` -- though `pip freeze` dumps *everything* currently installed, including transitive dependencies you never explicitly asked for, so many teams prefer to hand-maintain a shorter list of direct dependencies (leaving more thorough, fully-pinned lockfiles to dedicated tools like `pip-tools` or `poetry`) rather than committing a raw `pip freeze` dump without reviewing it first.

sections.heading: What PyPI Is
sections.body:
The Python Package Index (**PyPI**, at pypi.org) is the default public registry pip talks to -- a huge, open, community-run catalog where anyone can publish a package under a unique name. When you run `pip install requests`, pip is, by default, asking PyPI 'do you have a package named requests, and if so, what files make it up?', downloading whatever it finds, and installing it locally.

Two things are worth noting early. First, PyPI has essentially no vetting of what gets published: a package that exists and installs cleanly is no guarantee that the code is well-maintained, secure, or even does what its name suggests, so installing an unfamiliar package deserves a moment's thought about its popularity, maintenance activity, and whether you trust its source. Second, package names are a flat, global namespace on PyPI: once someone registers a name, no one else can publish under it, which is why common words tend to be taken already, and why 'typosquatting' (publishing malicious packages under names one character off from popular ones, hoping for a mistyped `pip install`) is a documented risk, not a theoretical one.

examples.title: A Package Containing Two Modules
examples.code:
# directory layout:
# my_project/
#     shapes/
#         __init__.py
#         circle.py
#         square.py
#     main.py

# shapes/circle.py
def area(radius):
    return 3.14159 * radius ** 2

# shapes/square.py
def area(side):
    return side ** 2

# main.py
from shapes import circle, square

print(circle.area(5))    # 78.53975
print(square.area(4))    # 16
examples.explanation: shapes is a package (a directory containing __init__.py) with two modules inside it, circle and square. Both modules happen to define a function named area, and that's fine, because they live in separate namespaces: main.py accesses them as circle.area and square.area, so there's no collision despite the identical function name. from shapes import circle, square pulls both modules (not the individual area functions) into main.py's namespace, which is why the calls still need the module prefix -- this is a middle ground between import shapes (requiring shapes.circle.area) and from shapes.circle import area (which would drop the prefix entirely, at the cost of losing the 'which module is this from' context if both circle.area and square.area were imported directly by name).

examples.title: From Freeform Installs to a Reproducible requirements.txt
examples.code:
# terminal session (not Python code):
# $ pip install requests
# $ pip install pandas==2.1.0
# $ pip freeze > requirements.txt

# resulting requirements.txt might contain far more than you expect,
# since pip freeze includes every transitive dependency too:
# requests==2.31.0
# pandas==2.1.0
# numpy==1.26.0        <- pandas depends on this; you never typed 'pip install numpy'
# python-dateutil==2.8.2
# pytz==2023.3
# six==1.16.0
# (abbreviated: requests also pulls in certifi, charset-normalizer, idna and urllib3,
# and pandas pulls in tzdata)

# a teammate on a fresh machine then runs:
# $ pip install -r requirements.txt
# ...which installs every listed package at those exact pinned versions
examples.explanation: Only requests and pandas were installed directly by name, but pip freeze captures the FULL, currently-installed dependency tree, including packages like numpy that pandas itself depends on internally -- these are called transitive dependencies. This is why some teams prefer to hand-maintain a short requirements.txt of just their direct dependencies (requests, pandas) and let pip resolve compatible versions of the rest at install time, rather than committing every transitive dependency's exact pinned version, which can make the file harder to read and can make upgrading a single direct dependency later require manually untangling which pinned transitive versions are still needed. Either approach solves the same core problem: a teammate on a different machine can run one command and end up with a working, reproducible set of dependencies, rather than guessing.

misconceptions.description: Any folder containing .py files is automatically a package you can import, as long as the files themselves are valid Python.
misconceptions.clarification: The conventional, always-reliable way to mark a directory as an importable package is to include an __init__.py file inside it. That's the explicit signal, historically required and still the clear convention, that tells Python 'treat this directory as a package.' Modern Python does support so-called namespace packages that can work without __init__.py under specific conditions, but relying on that behavior without understanding it is a common source of confusing ModuleNotFoundError or unexpected import behavior for beginners. The safe, predictable habit is: if you intend a directory to be imported as a package, give it an __init__.py.

misconceptions.description: pip install package_name installs the package globally for 'the computer' -- once installed, it's available to every project you ever work on, forever, the same way installing an application usually is.
misconceptions.clarification: Where pip actually installs a package depends on which Python installation (or, as covered in the next concept, which virtual environment) pip is currently associated with at the moment you run the command. Without any virtual environment active, yes, it typically goes into one shared, global installation that every project on the machine would see, but that's the problem virtual environments exist to solve, letting each project have its own private, independent set of installed packages instead of all sharing (and potentially conflicting over) one global set.

exercises.prompt: Given this project layout, main.py raises ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'circle' when run from inside my_project/. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
# project layout:
# my_project/
#     shapes/
#         __init__.py
#         circle.py      (defines: def area(radius): return 3.14159 * radius ** 2)
#     main.py

# main.py:
import circle
print(circle.area(5))
# run with: python main.py   (from inside my_project/)
# ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'circle'
hints: Where does circle.py live relative to main.py -- are they in the same directory?
Only the directory containing the script you run directly (my_project/, here) is added to sys.path automatically. Does that include shapes/ as a separate, directly importable location?
circle is a module INSIDE the shapes package: how do you tell Python to look for it there, rather than treating it as a top-level module of its own?
exercises.solutionCode:
# main.py:
from shapes import circle
print(circle.area(5))   # 78.53975
exercises.solutionExplanation: circle.py is not on sys.path: only my_project/ (the directory containing main.py, the script being run) is added automatically. shapes/ is a subdirectory, not a separate sys.path entry, so `import circle` fails: Python has no top-level module named circle to find. circle is only reachable through the shapes package that contains it, so `from shapes import circle` (or equivalently `import shapes.circle` followed by `shapes.circle.area(5)`) correctly tells Python to look for circle as a module living inside the shapes package, which it can resolve because shapes itself, as a package directory inside my_project/, is discoverable.

exercises.prompt: A project depends on requests at exactly version 2.31.0, and on pandas at version 2.0 or newer (any version 2.0+). Write the contents of a requirements.txt file capturing both constraints, and state the single pip command a new team member would run to install everything it lists.
hints: Version-pinning syntax goes directly after the package name, with no space, using a comparison operator.
'Exactly this version' and 'at least this version' use two different operators; they are not interchangeable.
The pip command that installs from a requirements file uses a specific flag to point at that file.
exercises.solutionCode:
# requirements.txt
requests==2.31.0
pandas>=2.0

# command to install everything listed:
# pip install -r requirements.txt
exercises.solutionExplanation: requests==2.31.0 pins that package to exactly version 2.31.0 using the == operator, matching the 'exactly this version' requirement. pandas>=2.0 uses the >= operator instead, allowing version 2.0 or any newer version, matching the 'at least this version' requirement. Using == here would have been too strict, since it would reject acceptable newer pandas releases. pip install -r requirements.txt reads the file line by line and installs each listed package at a version satisfying its constraint, which is the single command a teammate needs to reproduce this project's dependencies from scratch.

assessments.prompt: What primarily distinguishes a Python package from a Python module?
options: There is no real difference -- the terms are used interchangeably in Python
A package is faster to import than a module because it's precompiled
A module can only contain one function, while a package can contain many
A module is a .py file; a package is a directory (conventionally containing __init__.py) that can hold multiple modules and sub-packages
assessments.explanation: A module is a single .py file; a package is a directory that Python treats as a single importable unit, typically holding several modules (and possibly nested sub-packages), conventionally marked with an __init__.py. The “A package is faster to import…” option invents a performance claim with no basis. The “A module can only contain one function…” option is false: a single module can define any number of functions, classes, and variables. The “There is no real difference…” option is wrong; the two terms describe different things and the distinction matters for how you structure and import code.

assessments.prompt: Explain why a team commits requirements.txt to version control instead of just telling new developers which packages to pip install by hand, and describe one problem that can arise if a raw pip freeze output is committed without any review.
assessments.modelAnswer: requirements.txt makes a project's dependencies reproducible. Telling teammates by hand which packages and versions to install depends on everyone remembering correctly, and that list drifts out of date, gets forgotten, or is applied inconsistently across machines. The file is the single source of truth: anyone can recreate an equivalent set of dependencies with one command, pip install -r requirements.txt, and the dependency set used in development, testing, and production can be kept consistent and tracked in version control alongside the code that needs it. One problem with committing a raw, unreviewed pip freeze output: pip freeze lists EVERY installed package, including transitive dependencies pulled in by direct dependencies (a package like numpy that you never installed yourself but pandas depends on). The file ends up larger and more tightly pinned than necessary, harder to read, harder to tell which pins are required and which are incidental, and harder to upgrade one direct dependency safely without untangling which of the many pinned transitive versions must change with it.

assessments.prompt: A directory named `helpers` contains `math_utils.py` but no `__init__.py`. A script in the parent directory tries `from helpers import math_utils`. Following the convention covered in this lesson, what's the most reliable fix if this import doesn't behave as expected?
options: Move math_utils.py out of helpers/ and into the parent directory, abandoning the package structure entirely
Add a comment like # package at the top of math_utils.py
Add an (even empty) __init__.py file inside helpers/
Rename math_utils.py itself to __init__.py
assessments.explanation: The conventional, reliable signal that a directory should be treated as an importable package is the presence of an `__init__.py` file inside it, historically required and still the clear convention even though modern Python supports narrower 'namespace package' exceptions. Renaming the module itself to `__init__.py` (“Rename math_utils.py itself to __init__.py”) would destroy the module's identity and its `math_utils` name. Abandoning the package structure (“Move math_utils.py out of helpers/ and into…”) sidesteps the actual question rather than fixing the package. A plain comment (“Add a comment like # package…”) has no effect on Python's import machinery at all.

assessments.prompt: A requirements.txt file contains the line `pandas>=2.0`. Which of these installed versions would satisfy that constraint?
options: Any version at all, since >= is ignored by pip
Only exactly 2.0, and no other version
assessments.explanation: `>=2.0` means 'version 2.0 or any newer version': 2.3.1 is newer than 2.0, so it satisfies the constraint. 1.9.0 is older than 2.0, so it does not. The “Only exactly 2.0, and no other version” option is wrong because >= allows versions greater than 2.0 as well, not just exactly 2.0; that would require ==2.0 instead. The “Any version at all, since >=…” option is wrong: pip respects version-comparison operators in requirements.txt; that's the point of writing one.

assessments.prompt: Why is 'typosquatting' considered a documented risk with pip and PyPI, rather than a purely theoretical concern?
options: PyPI performs essentially no vetting of published packages, and package names form a flat global namespace, so someone can publish a malicious package under a name one character off from a popular one, hoping for a mistyped install command
pip does not support version pinning at all, making it impossible to know what was actually installed
pip automatically installs whichever package is most popular for a given search term, regardless of the exact name typed
PyPI requires all package names to be extremely short, which makes typos statistically inevitable
assessments.explanation: PyPI's open, essentially unvetted publishing model means a package existing and installing cleanly is no guarantee it's legitimate or safe, and because package names are a flat, global namespace, an attacker can register a name that's just one character or one common misspelling away from a popular package, banking on someone mistyping `pip install` and installing the malicious lookalike instead. pip doesn't auto-correct or guess at intended package names (“pip automatically installs whichever package is most…”), PyPI imposes no such short-name requirement (“PyPI requires all package names…”), and pip does support version pinning (“pip does not support version pinning…”) -- none of those describe the mechanism behind typosquatting.

concepts.title: Virtual Environments
concepts.description: A virtual environment gives each project its own isolated Python interpreter and site-packages directory, solving the problem of different projects on the same machine needing incompatible versions of the same package.
learningObjectives: Explain why isolating dependencies per project matters, using a concrete version-conflict scenario.
Create and activate a virtual environment using the venv module.
Diagnose the classic 'installed but not found' bug caused by installing a package before activating the intended virtual environment.
Explain how virtual environments and requirements.txt work together to make a project's setup reproducible.

sections.heading: Why Isolate Dependencies Per Project
sections.body:
Without any isolation, every `pip install` on your machine targets one global Python installation shared by every project you work on. That's fine until two projects need incompatible versions of the same package: Project A depends on `requests==2.10.0` because some function signature it relies on changed in later versions, while Project B needs `requests>=2.28` for a security fix or a feature it uses. There is only one `requests` installed globally at any moment, so installing the version one project needs overwrites the version the other needs, and you can't satisfy both projects from a single shared installation.

This isn't a rare edge case; it's the default state of affairs the moment you work on more than one nontrivial Python project on the same machine, which is why isolating dependencies **per project** is treated as baseline practice, not an advanced technique. A **virtual environment** (venv) is the standard solution: a self-contained, isolated environment with its own interpreter entry point and its own private `site-packages` directory, associated with one project. Packages installed 'into' a virtual environment go into that private directory, completely independent of both the global Python installation and every other project's own virtual environment. Two projects can each have their own virtual environment, each with its own independently chosen version of `requests`, and neither ever knows the other one exists.

sections.heading: Creating and Activating a Virtual Environment
sections.body:
Python's standard library includes the `venv` module for this purpose (no separate installation needed, unlike some third-party alternatives). Creating one is a single command, typically run once per project, from inside the project's own directory:

```
python -m venv .venv
```

This creates a directory (commonly named `.venv` or `venv`) containing its own `python` executable (a symlink on macOS/Linux, a copy on Windows) and an empty `site-packages`. Creating it doesn't change how your terminal behaves yet; for that you need to **activate** it, which is a shell-specific command:

```
# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

# Windows (PowerShell)
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

Activation modifies your *current shell session's* PATH (and a couple of other environment variables) so that, for the rest of that session, plain `python` and `pip` commands resolve to the virtual environment's own copies instead of whatever global Python is otherwise installed on the machine. Your prompt typically changes to show the active environment's name (often `(.venv)` prepended) as a visual reminder that you're 'inside' it. Deactivating (`deactivate`) reverses this, restoring the shell to whatever it pointed at before.

sections.heading: The Classic Mistake: Installing Before Activating
sections.body:
The most common practical mistake with virtual environments has a misleading symptom: running `pip install some_package` **before** activating the project's virtual environment in that terminal session. Nothing about that command visibly fails; pip downloads and installs `some_package` as asked, with no error. The catch is *where*: with no virtual environment active, `pip` and `python` point at the global installation, so the package gets installed into the shared global one instead of the isolated environment you meant. (On some systems, such as recent Debian and Ubuntu releases and Homebrew's Python, pip refuses global installs with an `externally-managed-environment` error, so there the mistake announces itself; on many setups it simply succeeds.)

The confusing part comes next: you then activate the virtual environment and try to `import some_package`, and get `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'some_package'` -- which reads like the install failed, even though it succeeded a moment ago. It didn't fail; it installed into the wrong place, because the venv wasn't active *at the time you ran pip install*. This is why it's worth building the habit of checking which Python/pip you're using before installing anything new in a project you know has its own venv: `which python` (macOS/Linux) or `where python` (Windows) shows the path currently in use, and it should point *inside* your project's `.venv` directory, not at a system-wide location, before you trust that a fresh `pip install` is going where you think it's going.

sections.heading: Connecting Back to requirements.txt
sections.body:
Virtual environments and `requirements.txt` are two halves of the same reproducibility story: a virtual environment gives each project its own isolated place to install packages into, and `requirements.txt` records *what* should be installed there, so that isolation can be recreated on any machine, by any teammate, at any time. The standard project setup routine is: create a fresh virtual environment, activate it, then `pip install -r requirements.txt` to populate that empty, isolated environment with exactly the dependencies the project declares -- rather than either sharing one global installation across every project (the problem venvs solve) or relying purely on word-of-mouth about which packages to install (the problem requirements.txt solves).

Skipping the venv and just running `pip install -r requirements.txt` globally 'works,' in the narrow sense that the imports will succeed, but it reintroduces the cross-project version-conflict problem venvs exist to prevent, the moment you work on a second project with different needs.

examples.title: Creating, Activating, and Verifying a Virtual Environment
examples.code:
$ cd my_project
$ python -m venv .venv
$ which python
/usr/bin/python
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ which python
/home/amy/my_project/.venv/bin/python
(.venv) $ pip install requests
(.venv) $ pip freeze > requirements.txt
(.venv) $ deactivate
$ which python
/usr/bin/python
examples.explanation: Right after creating .venv, which python still reports the global system interpreter -- creating the venv directory alone does not change the current shell's PATH. Only after source .venv/bin/activate does which python change to point inside the project's own .venv/bin directory, confirming the virtual environment is active for this shell session. With it active, pip install requests installs into .venv's private site-packages, completely separate from the global installation, and pip freeze > requirements.txt records exactly that (isolated) set of installed packages. deactivate reverses the PATH change, and which python afterward reports the original global interpreter again -- the isolation and its reversal are both just PATH manipulation, nothing deeper.

examples.title: The Install-Before-Activate Trap, Concretely
examples.code:
$ cd my_project
$ python -m venv .venv
$ pip install pandas          # venv NOT active yet -- this installs globally!
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ python -c "import pandas"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'
(.venv) $ pip install pandas   # now it actually goes into .venv
(.venv) $ python -c "import pandas"
# no error this time -- works fine
examples.explanation: The first pip install pandas runs before the venv is activated, so it succeeds, with no error message, by installing pandas into the global Python installation, not into .venv. Once .venv is activated and python -c "import pandas" is run, Python looks inside the now-active virtual environment's own, still-empty site-packages, doesn't find pandas there (it's sitting in the global installation instead), and raises ModuleNotFoundError. This is the symptom of the install-before-activate mistake: the earlier pip install succeeded, just in the wrong location, which makes the later 'it's not found' error feel contradictory until you notice the venv wasn't active yet when the install actually ran. Running pip install pandas again, now with the venv active, correctly installs it into .venv's site-packages, and the import succeeds.

misconceptions.description: Creating a virtual environment with python -m venv .venv is enough by itself -- packages installed afterward will automatically go into it.
misconceptions.clarification: Creating the .venv directory only builds the isolated environment; it does not change anything about your current shell session. Until you explicitly activate it (source .venv/bin/activate on macOS/Linux, or .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 on Windows), your shell's python and pip commands still point at whatever they pointed at before -- typically the global installation -- so any pip install run in between creating and activating the venv goes to the wrong place entirely.
misconceptions.fact: Creating the .venv directory only builds the isolated environment; it does not change anything about your current shell session.

misconceptions.description: If pip install completes with no error message, the package was definitely installed into your project's intended virtual environment.
misconceptions.clarification: Success just means the install went wherever pip currently points at that moment -- which depends on whether the intended virtual environment was actually active when the command ran, not on whether you merely intended to be using it. pip has no way of knowing which environment you meant to target; it only knows which one is currently active (or, absent that, the global one). Success and 'went to the right place' are two different things, which is why checking which python/where python before installing, in a project you know has its own venv, is a useful habit rather than unnecessary caution.

exercises.prompt: A developer creates a virtual environment, installs a package, activates the environment, and then can't import that package. Find the bug in this sequence of commands.
exercises.code:
$ cd my_project
$ python -m venv .venv
$ pip install requests
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ python -c "import requests"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'
hints: Look at the ORDER of these commands -- when exactly does source .venv/bin/activate happen relative to pip install requests?
pip install requests didn't raise any error, so it definitely installed requests SOMEWHERE. The question is where.
Without an active virtual environment, pip and python point at the global installation, not at .venv, even though .venv already exists as a directory at that point.
exercises.solutionCode:
$ cd my_project
$ python -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ pip install requests
(.venv) $ python -c "import requests"
# no error -- works fine
exercises.solutionExplanation: In the original sequence, pip install requests runs BEFORE source .venv/bin/activate, so at that moment no virtual environment is active and pip installs requests into the global Python installation instead of into .venv. Activating the venv afterward doesn't retroactively move that already-installed package -- it just switches which python/pip the shell uses going forward. So when python -c "import requests" then runs inside the now-active (but still requests-less) .venv, it correctly reports ModuleNotFoundError, because requests was never actually installed into THIS environment's site-packages. The fix is to activate the virtual environment first, and only then run pip install requests, so the install actually lands inside .venv.

exercises.prompt: What does each `which python` call print, given the commands run between them? Assume the project lives at /home/amy/my_project.
exercises.code:
$ cd /home/amy/my_project
$ which python
/usr/bin/python
$ python -m venv .venv
$ which python
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ which python
(.venv) $ deactivate
$ which python
hints: Does simply creating a venv directory change your shell's PATH at all, or does something else have to happen first?
Compare the path right after python -m venv .venv to the path right after source .venv/bin/activate. What changed between those two points?
deactivate is designed to reverse whatever activate did to the shell's PATH.
exercises.expectedAnswer: /usr/bin/python, then /usr/bin/python again (unchanged -- creating the venv doesn't touch PATH), then /home/amy/my_project/.venv/bin/python (after activation), then /usr/bin/python again (after deactivate restores the original PATH).
exercises.solutionExplanation: The second which python call happens right after python -m venv .venv, which only creates the .venv directory and its contents -- it does not modify the shell's PATH at all, so which python still reports the original global interpreter, /usr/bin/python, unchanged. After source .venv/bin/activate, the shell's PATH is modified to put .venv/bin first, so which python now reports /home/amy/my_project/.venv/bin/python, the virtual environment's own interpreter. After deactivate, the PATH modification is reversed back to what it was before activation, so which python reports /usr/bin/python once more, identical to the very first call.

assessments.prompt: A developer runs `pip install flask` without having activated any virtual environment first, and it completes with no errors. What actually happened?
options: flask was installed into the global/system Python installation
pip refuses to install anything unless a virtual environment is active, so nothing was actually installed
The install silently failed despite showing no error message
flask was automatically installed into the most recently created virtual environment on the machine, even without activation
assessments.explanation: pip and python always resolve to whichever installation is currently on PATH -- with no virtual environment active, that's the global/system installation, so the install succeeds there. The “pip refuses to install anything unless…” option is wrong: pip has no such restriction and will happily install globally. The “flask was automatically installed into the most…” option is wrong: pip has no notion of a 'most recently created' venv to fall back to; it only knows about whatever is currently active (or the global installation, absent that). The “The install silently failed despite showing no error message” option is wrong: the install did succeed, just in the global location rather than an intended, but not-yet-active, virtual environment.

assessments.prompt: Two projects on the same laptop need different, incompatible versions of the same package: Project A requires requests==2.10.0, Project B requires requests>=2.28. Explain how virtual environments solve this, and what would go wrong if the developer instead just used the single global Python installation for both projects.
assessments.modelAnswer: Without virtual environments, both projects share one global Python installation and one global site-packages directory, which can hold only ONE version of requests at a time. Installing requests==2.10.0 for Project A leaves Project B without the newer version it needs, and installing requests>=2.28 for Project B overwrites the 2.10.0 install Project A depends on. Nothing can satisfy both requirements from a single shared installation; switching projects would mean reinstalling a different version each time, and forgetting to would run at least one project against the wrong version. Virtual environments solve this by giving each project its own private site-packages directory, created once with python -m venv and activated whenever you work on that project. Project A's environment can have requests==2.10.0 and Project B's separate environment can have requests>=2.28, and neither is aware of or affected by the other, so both projects' version requirements are satisfied at once, with no reinstalling when switching.

assessments.prompt: A developer activates project_A's virtual environment in one terminal and runs `pip install requests`. In a completely separate terminal, project_B's own (different) virtual environment is active, and project_B never had requests installed. Running `pip list` in that second terminal -- does 'requests' show up?
options: Yes, but only the very first time pip list is run after the install
No -- each virtual environment has its own independent site-packages
Only if project_B's virtual environment was created after project_A's
Yes -- pip list always reports every package installed anywhere on the machine, across every environment
assessments.explanation: pip list reports what's installed in whichever Python environment pip is currently pointed at, and that's determined by which environment is active in that terminal session, not by what's been installed anywhere else on the machine. project_A's and project_B's virtual environments each have their own separate, independent site-packages directory; installing requests into project_A's does not add it to project_B's in any way. So the second terminal's pip list, scoped to project_B's own environment, doesn't show a package that was never installed there.

assessments.prompt:
```
(.venv) $ deactivate
$ pip install requests
```
Where does `requests` get installed by that second command?
options: Nowhere -- pip refuses to run at all without an active virtual environment
Into both the global installation and .venv at the same time
Into the global/system Python installation
Into the now-inactive .venv, since pip remembers the last environment it was pointed at
assessments.explanation: deactivate reverses what activate did to the shell's PATH, restoring it to whatever it pointed at beforehand -- typically the global/system Python. Once deactivated, pip has no memory of the environment that was previously active; it simply resolves to whatever's currently on PATH, which after deactivation is the global installation. So the pip install that runs after deactivate goes to the global site-packages, not back into .venv, and pip runs normally outside any virtual environment -- there's no restriction requiring one to be active.

assessments.prompt: A developer skips creating a virtual environment entirely and instead just runs `pip install -r requirements.txt` directly against the global Python installation, for every project they work on. What problem does this fail to solve?
options: It prevents requirements.txt from recording accurate version numbers
pip install -r raises an error whenever no virtual environment is active
Nothing -- as long as requirements.txt is used, the setup is already just as isolated as a virtual environment would provide
It reintroduces the exact cross-project version-conflict problem virtual environments exist to prevent
assessments.explanation: requirements.txt only records *what* to install; it says nothing about *where*. Running pip install -r requirements.txt with no virtual environment active still installs everything into the one shared global site-packages, exactly like any other pip install without an active venv. If a second project later needs an incompatible version of something the first project also depends on, the same version-conflict problem virtual environments were designed to prevent reappears, unaffected by the fact that a requirements.txt file was used. requirements.txt (what to install) and virtual environments (where, in isolation, to install it) solve two different, complementary halves of the reproducibility problem -- using one doesn't substitute for the other.
